chief_complaint: excruciating burning pain, swelling, and color changes in right wrist and hand for 3 months after a fracture
hpi_details: 3-month history of constant, agonizing, burning and crushing pain affecting her entire right hand and wrist, far out of proportion to the inciting injury. Sustained a simple right distal radius Colles fracture 4 months ago after slipping on ice, which was treated conservatively with plaster cast immobilization and healed radiographically within 6 weeks. Since the cast was removed 3 months ago, the right hand has become swollen, exquisitely hypersensitive where even the light touch of a bedsheet or breeze causes agonizing pain (allodynia). Reports strange vasomotor and sweating changes: her right hand alternates between turning bright red and throbbing hot, to turning mottled, purple, and icy cold compared to the normal left hand. Skin over the fingers looks shiny, taut, and swollen, with rapid nail growth and stiffness in all finger joints.
ideas: thinks the orthopedic surgeon set the bone incorrectly and trapped a major nerve inside her wrist
concerns: terrified she will never be able to use her right hand again and will lose her job as an illustrator
expectations: wants surgical re-breaking of the wrist bone or nerve surgery to cure the burning agony immediately
pmh: right distal radius fracture 4 months ago, mild generalized anxiety
medications: paracetamol, ibuprofen, and codeine with zero reduction in neuropathic burning
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks socially, freelance digital illustrator, right-hand dominant

clinical_knowledge.topic: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes explaining the neuro-inflammatory central and peripheral sensitization mechanisms of CRPS empathetically, while avoiding unnecessary invasive procedures that may exacerbate symptoms, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating burning pain, swelling, and color changes in right wrist and hand for 3 months after a fracture

Key HPI features: 3-month history of constant, agonizing, burning and crushing pain affecting her entire right hand and wrist, far out of proportion to the inciting injury. Sustained a simple right distal radius Colles fracture 4 months ago after slipping on ice, which was treated conservatively with plaster cast immobilization and healed radiographically within 6 weeks. Since the cast was removed 3 months ago, the right hand has become swollen, exquisitely hypersensitive where even the light touch of a bedsheet or breeze causes agonizing pain (allodynia). Reports strange vasomotor and sweating changes: her right hand alternates between turning bright red and throbbing hot, to turning mottled, purple, and icy cold compared to the normal left hand. Skin over the fingers looks shiny, taut, and swollen, with rapid nail growth and stiffness in all finger joints.

Objective/Exam findings: Apply Budapest Diagnostic Criteria for CRPS: inspect and compare both hands simultaneously. Continuing pain disproportionate to inciting event. Sensory: profound mechanical allodynia (light cotton wool touch over right dorsum provokes severe pain) and hyperalgesia. Vasomotor: visible skin temperature asymmetry (right hand measured >2°C cooler/warmer than left) and mottling/erythema. Sudomotor/Oedema: non-pitting dorsal wrist/hand oedema and hyperhidrosis. Motor/Trophic: decreased right hand grip strength, decreased finger range of motion (contractures), shiny taut skin, and brittle/rapid nail changes. Plain X-ray right hand: shows patchy, periarticular osteopenia / Sudeck's atrophy. Nerve conduction studies: normal without major nerve trunk transection (confirms CRPS Type I vs Type II where major nerve injury exists).
Relevant background/PMH: right distal radius fracture 4 months ago, mild generalized anxiety
Current medications: paracetamol, ibuprofen, and codeine with zero reduction in neuropathic burning
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to CRPS Type II (confirmed major nerve injury) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapidly progressive swelling with signs of infection — needs to be distinguished from CRPS by exam and labs.
management_principles: Explain the neuro-inflammatory central and peripheral sensitization mechanisms of CRPS empathetically, clarifying that the bone is healed and that unnecessary invasive procedures may worsen symptoms

Multidisciplinary functional rehabilitation: urgent referral to specialized hand/neuropathic pain occupational and physical therapy for gentle, progressive desensitization (mirror box therapy, tactile desensitization, graded motor imagery, active range-of-motion exercises)
Neuropathic pain pharmacological ladder: initiate pregabalin starting 75mg BID or gabapentin, combined with duloxetine 30mg-60mg OD or tricyclic antidepressants
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 41F presents with chronic agonizing neuropathic pain, allodynia, vasomotor instability, sudomotor changes, and joint stiffness in right hand/wrist 3 months post-distal radius fracture.
reference_soap.objective: Apply Budapest Diagnostic Criteria for CRPS: inspect and compare both hands simultaneously. Continuing pain disproportionate to inciting event. Sensory: profound mechanical allodynia (light cotton wool touch over right dorsum provokes severe pain) and hyperalgesia. Vasomotor: visible skin temperature asymmetry (right hand measured >2°C cooler/warmer than left) and mottling/erythema. Sudomotor/Oedema: non-pitting dorsal wrist/hand oedema and hyperhidrosis. Motor/Trophic: decreased right hand grip strength, decreased finger range of motion (contractures), shiny taut skin, and brittle/rapid nail changes. Plain X-ray right hand: shows patchy, periarticular osteopenia / Sudeck's atrophy. Nerve conduction studies: normal without major nerve trunk transection (confirms CRPS Type I vs Type II where major nerve injury exists).
reference_soap.assessment: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I / Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy - RSD) of the right upper limb post-distal radius fracture. DDx: CRPS Type II (causalgia with confirmed major nerve injury), peripheral nerve entrapment (carpal tunnel syndrome), thoracic outlet syndrome, post-traumatic osteomyelitis, inflammatory arthritis.
reference_soap.plan: Explain the neuro-inflammatory central and peripheral sensitization mechanisms of CRPS empathetically, clarifying that the bone is healed and that unnecessary invasive procedures may worsen symptoms. Arrange prompt referral to specialized hand/neuropathic pain occupational and physical therapy for gentle, progressive desensitization (mirror box therapy, tactile desensitization, graded motor imagery, active range-of-motion exercises). Consider neuropathic pain pharmacotherapy and other interventions in collaboration with an appropriate specialist, tailored to comorbidities and local guidance. Refer to a multidisciplinary pain clinic if symptoms are refractory.

learning_objectives: Apply the Budapest Clinical Diagnostic Criteria to diagnose Complex Regional Pain Syndrome based on sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor, and trophic categories
Differentiate CRPS Type I (no major nerve injury) from CRPS Type II (causalgia with documented major peripheral nerve injury)
Explain why unnecessary surgery may exacerbate neuropathic sensitization in active CRPS
Formulate a multidisciplinary pain rehabilitation plan prioritizing early desensitization, mirror box therapy, and neuropathic pharmacotherapy

teaching.diagnosis: Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I (CRPS I)
teaching.one_liner: A dysregulated pain and autonomic response after a minor injury — here a healed wrist fracture — causing burning pain wildly out of proportion to the injury, along with color changes, temperature changes, swelling, and extreme sensitivity to light touch.
differentials: CRPS Type II (confirmed major nerve injury)
red_flags: Rapidly progressive swelling with signs of infection — needs to be distinguished from CRPS by exam and labs

must_ask.say: Is the pain much worse than you'd expect for a healed fracture?
Does even light touch, like a bedsheet or breeze, cause severe pain?
Does your hand change color or temperature compared to the other side?
When was your wrist fracture, and when did this pain start after the cast came off?
Have you noticed changes in your skin texture or nail growth?
